submission.natural_language_explanation: Fires on clauses that predicate a concrete physical part, attribute or covering of a tangible body - animals, people, plants and everyday food/materials ('The bear has sharp claws and thick fur', 'The cow has a long tail', 'The plant has green leaves', 'His face was covered in mud', 'She peeled the potatoes'), usually peaking on ' has', the attribute adjective, the body-part or food noun, or the ' in'/' of' that joins a substance to a surface. It does not fire when the same frames carry an abstract, mental or institutional subject or predicate ('The report has several sections', 'The plan was covered in detail', 'She considered the options'), nor on clauses about inert artefacts being mechanically handled ('He opened the window', 'He turned the key in the lock'); those are its main leftovers among concrete text, together with cooking clauses without a body/material term (about half of them stay below the activity line).

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
Field notes from the Aldergrove reserve, compiled over three weeks by the volunteer survey team. The mornings were cold and the paths muddy, so most recording was done between nine and eleven, once the frost had lifted. On the first visit the team walked the eastern fence line, counting rabbit burrows and noting where the hedge had been cut back. Nothing unusual was recorded beyond a pair of kestrels hunting over the meadow.

The second visit produced the first real surprise. A young roe deer stood near the pond, apparently unbothered by the group, and watched for several minutes before moving off into the bracken. The volunteers logged the sighting and carried on towards the wood, where the ground was soft and the trees still held their leaves.

By the third week the survey had moved to the northern fields, where the grass is longer and the ground holds water. The team spent an hour following the stream and marking the places where the bank had collapsed. A heron was fishing at the bend, and a small group of ducks moved downstream whenever the volunteers came close. Two of the planned visits were cancelled because of heavy rain, and one afternoon was lost when the weather turned and nobody had brought the right tools. The team asked the estate office for a spare key and expects to have it before the next survey.

The most interesting record came on the final morning, when the group reached the old barn at the top of the field. The barn was old and the floorboards were rotten, so the volunteers kept to the edge of the building. Near the doorway they found a young goat that had wandered in from the neighbouring smallholding. The goat had a matted coat and a crooked horn, and its hooves were caked in mud from the yard. It stood quite still while the team checked it for injuries. Eventually a farmer arrived, lifted the animal into the back of his truck and drove it home.

The full list of species recorded during the survey will be added to the reserve database before the end of the month. Anyone who wants to join the next round of visits should speak to the warden, who keeps a sign-up sheet in the visitor centre and can lend out spare boots and clipboards.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Long-context, different-genre holdout (field notes) with ' had' clauses predicating a matted coat, a crooked horn and hooves caked in mud deep inside a 500-plus-token passage, predicted active by the hypothesis.
